subject: maths
title: Chapter 11 · Test 2
summary: Chapter 11 test 2: searching and sorting algorithms, recurrence rules, iteration and approximation — 15 questions.
body: This test covers Chapter 11 · Algorithmic thinking: linear and binary search, bubble sort and selection sort, counting comparisons, recurrence rules, the Babylonian method for square roots, fixed-point iteration, the halving method and stopping rules. Allow about 25 minutes, no notes, no calculator unless the question says. Some questions show the list or graph in a diagram — read it carefully. Work each question out on paper before you look at the options, and write your steps so you can find where you went wrong.

questions.prompt: Linear search is used to find 40 in the list shown in the diagram. How many comparisons are made, including the one that finds 40?
questions.explanation: Linear search checks from the left: 8, 19, 3, 25, 12, 40 — 40 is found on comparison 6. 5 forgets to count the comparison that finds it.
steps: Linear search starts with the first item and checks each item in turn.
The items checked are 8, 19, 3, 25, 12, 40, so 40 is found on comparison 6.

mistakes.A: Step 2: count the comparison with 40 itself as well — that is the one that finds it.
mistakes.B: Step 2: linear search stops as soon as it finds 40; it does not check the rest of the list.
mistakes.C: Step 1: linear search starts at the first item on the left, not at the end of the list.

questions.diagram_alt: A list of 8 boxes holding 8, 19, 3, 25, 12, 40, 7, 16, with positions 1 to 8 underneath.

questions.prompt: Bubble sort is used to put the list in the diagram into increasing order. What is the list after the first comparison?
questions.explanation: 9 and 4 are out of order, so they swap: 4, 9, 6, 1. 4, 6, 1, 9 is the list after the whole pass.
steps: Compare the first pair, 9 and 4: 9 is bigger, so they are in the wrong order.
Swap them: 4, 9, 6, 1.

mistakes.A: Step 2: 9 is bigger than 4, so they are in the wrong order and must swap.
mistakes.C: Step 2: one comparison can only swap one pair — the list is not fully sorted yet.
mistakes.D: Step 2: that is the list after the whole first pass. Only one comparison has been made.

questions.diagram_alt: A list of 4 boxes holding 9, 4, 6, 1, with the first two boxes highlighted for comparison.

questions.prompt: A sequence follows the rule uₙ₊₁ = 2uₙ − 3 with u₀ = 7. Find u₂.
questions.explanation: u₁ = 2 × 7 − 3 = 11 and u₂ = 2 × 11 − 3 = 19. 11 stops after one step.
steps: u₁ = 2 × 7 − 3 = 11 — substitute u₀ into the rule.
u₂ = 2 × 11 − 3 = 19 — feed u₁ back into the rule.

mistakes.A: Step 1: 11 is only u₁. Use the rule a second time to get u₂.
mistakes.B: Step 1: multiply by 2 first, then subtract 3 — you did them in the wrong order.
mistakes.D: Step 2: that is u₃ — you used the rule one time too many.

questions.prompt: The halving method is used on f(x) = x² − 7. The diagram shows f(2), f(2.5) and f(3). After this halving, which interval contains the solution?
questions.explanation: The sign changes in the interval 2.5 to 3, so the graph crosses zero there. 2 to 2.5 has no sign change.
steps: Look at the signs: f(2) = −3 is negative, f(3) = 2 is positive and f(2.5) = −0.75 is negative.
The sign changes between 2.5 and 3, so the solution is in the interval 2.5 to 3.

mistakes.B: Step 2: keep the half where the signs are DIFFERENT. f(2) and f(2.5) have the same sign.
mistakes.C: Step 2: after finding f(2.5), update the interval to half its width.
mistakes.D: Step 2: only one halving is asked for — you cannot narrow it further without another function value.

questions.diagram_alt: A number line from 2 to 3 with f(2) = −3, f(2.5) = −0.75 and f(3) = 2 marked.

questions.prompt: Binary search is used to find 38 in the sorted list shown. The middle position is (low + high) ÷ 2, rounded down. Which numbers are compared with 38, in order?
questions.explanation: Halving from the middle each time compares 29, 42, 31, 38. Rounding the middle up instead gives 31, 47, 42, 38.
steps: Middle of 1 to 12 is position 6, which holds 29. 38 is bigger, so keep positions 7 to 12.
Middle of 7 to 12 is position 9, which holds 42. 38 is smaller, so keep positions 7 to 8.
Middle of 7 to 8 is position 7, which holds 31. 38 is bigger, so keep position 8.
Position 8 is all that is left; it holds 38 — found. So the order is 29, 42, 31, 38.

mistakes.A: Step 2: when (low + high) ÷ 2 is not a whole number, round it DOWN, not up.
mistakes.C: Step 2: after the first look, find the middle of the part that is left — do not step along one item at a time.
mistakes.D: Step 1: that is linear search. Binary search starts by looking at the middle position.

questions.diagram_alt: A sorted list of 12 boxes: 5, 9, 14, 18, 23, 29, 31, 38, 42, 47, 53, 56, with positions 1 to 12 underneath.

questions.prompt: The diagram shows the list 8, 3, 6, 1, 5, 2 before bubble sort starts (sorting into increasing order). What is the list after the first pass?
questions.explanation: Walking along and swapping each out-of-order pair gives 3, 6, 1, 5, 2, 8 — the largest value, 8, ends at the back. 3, 1, 5, 2, 6, 8 is after two passes.
steps: Compare 8 and 3: swap → 3, 8, 6, 1, 5, 2. Compare 8 and 6: swap → 3, 6, 8, 1, 5, 2. Compare 8 and 1: swap → 3, 6, 1, 8, 5, 2.
Compare 8 and 5: swap → 3, 6, 1, 5, 8, 2. Compare 8 and 2: swap → 3, 6, 1, 5, 2, 8.

mistakes.B: Step 2: one pass does not sort the whole list — it only makes sure the largest value reaches the end.
mistakes.C: Step 2: that is after the SECOND pass. Stop after one walk along the list.
mistakes.D: Step 1: keep going after the first swap — compare every neighbouring pair along the list.

questions.prompt: A sorted list has 200 items. What is the greatest number of comparisons binary search could need?
questions.explanation: Find the smallest k with 2ᵏ ≥ 201: 2⁷ = 128 is too small and 2⁸ = 256 is enough, so 8.
steps: Binary search worst case: the smallest whole number k with 2ᵏ ≥ n + 1 = 201.
2⁷ = 128 is too small, but 2⁸ = 256 ≥ 201, so the answer is 8.

mistakes.A: Step 1: binary search halves the list every look — 100 is just half the list after one look.
mistakes.B: Step 1: 200 is the worst case for linear search, not binary search.
mistakes.D: Step 2: 2⁷ = 128 is less than 201, so 7 looks are not enough. Round up, not down.

questions.prompt: A bank account follows Bₙ₊₁ = 1.005Bₙ + 200 each month (200 dollars deposited each month), where B₀ = $4000. Find B₂, the balance after 2 months.
questions.explanation: B₁ = 1.005 × 4000 + 200 = 4220.00 and B₂ = 1.005 × 4220.00 + 200 = 4441.10. $4440.00 wrongly earns interest on the original balance both months.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the rule multiplies by 1.005 each month — you left out the interest.
mistakes.B: Step 2: the interest in month 2 is on $4220.00, not on the original $4000.
mistakes.C: Step 1: $4220.00 is only after one month. Use the rule again for B₂.

questions.prompt: The iteration xₙ₊₁ = √(3xₙ + 10) settles at a value of x. Which equation does that value solve?
questions.explanation: At the fixed point the new and old values are equal, which leads to x² − 3x − 10 = 0 (its positive solution is 5).
steps: When the iterates settle at x, the rule says x = √(3x + 10).
Square both sides: x² = 3x + 10, then move everything to one side: x² − 3x − 10 = 0.

mistakes.A: Step 2: moving 3x + 10 to the left side changes both signs to minus.
mistakes.C: Step 2: subtract 10 from both sides, so the constant becomes −10.
mistakes.D: Step 1: a fixed point means x = √(3x + 10). Square BOTH sides to remove the square root.

questions.prompt: Selection sort is used on the list 9, 6, 3, 8, 4, shown in the diagram (sorting into increasing order). What is the list after the second pass?
questions.explanation: Two passes place 3 and then 4 at the front: 3, 4, 9, 8, 6. 3, 6, 4, 8, 9 is what bubble sort gives after two passes.
steps: Pass 1: the smallest of all is 3 — swap it with the first item, 9: 3, 6, 9, 8, 4.
Pass 2: the smallest of 6, 9, 8, 4 is 4 — swap it with 6: 3, 4, 9, 8, 6.

mistakes.A: Step 2: two passes only fix the first two positions — the rest is not sorted yet.
mistakes.B: Step 1: that is after one pass. Do a second pass on the items after the first.
mistakes.C: Step 1: that is bubble sort after two passes. Selection sort moves the smallest remaining item to the front.

questions.prompt: A sorted list holds 250 names, and a name that is NOT in the list is searched for. How many more comparisons does linear search need than binary search, in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Linear search checks all 250. Binary search needs the smallest k with 2ᵏ ≥ 251, which is 8 (2⁸ = 256). 250 − 8 = 242.
steps: Linear search: a missing name means all 250 names are checked.
Binary search: 2⁷ = 128 is too small, 2⁸ = 256 ≥ 251, so 8 comparisons.
Difference: 250 − 8 = 242.

mistakes.B: Step 1: the worst case for linear search is all 250 items, not half of them.
mistakes.C: Step 2: 2⁷ = 128 is less than 251, so binary search needs 8 looks, not 7.
mistakes.D: Step 2: binary search halves the list on every look — it needs far fewer than half the items.

questions.prompt: The halving method starts with the interval 5 to 6. How many halvings are needed to make the interval narrower than 0.0001?
questions.explanation: After n halvings the width is 1 ÷ 2ⁿ, so we need 2ⁿ greater than 10000: 2¹³ = 8192 is too small and 2¹⁴ = 16384 works, so 14.
steps: After n halvings the width is 1 ÷ 2ⁿ, so 2ⁿ must be greater than 1 ÷ 0.0001 = 10000.
2¹³ = 8192 is too small; 2¹⁴ = 16384 is big enough, so 14 halvings.

mistakes.A: Step 1: halving does not add one decimal place each time — each step only halves the width.
mistakes.B: Step 2: after 13 halvings the width is 1 ÷ 8192 ≈ 0.00012, which is not yet narrower than 0.0001.
mistakes.D: Step 1: 10000 is how many pieces of width 0.0001 fit in the interval. Each halving doubles the pieces, so far fewer steps are needed.

questions.prompt: A loan of $15 000 follows Lₙ₊₁ = 1.006Lₙ − 900, where n is the number of months (0.6% interest per month and a $900 repayment). After how many months is the balance first below $12 500?
questions.explanation: Working month by month, L₃ ≈ $12 555.39 is still above $12 500 but L₄ ≈ $11 730.72 is below, so 4 months. Ignoring the interest gives 3.

mistakes.A: Step 1: the rule multiplies by the interest factor before taking off the repayment — without interest the balance falls too quickly.
mistakes.B: Step 2: L₀ is the starting balance, not month 1. Count from L₁.
mistakes.C: Step 1: 0.6% per month is ×1.006, not ×1.06. With ×1.06 the interest would cancel the repayment every month.

questions.prompt: A computer takes 5 seconds to bubble sort 2000 items in the worst case. Roughly how long would it take to bubble sort 4000 items in the worst case?
questions.explanation: Comparisons = n(n − 1) ÷ 2, roughly n² ÷ 2, so 2 times the items is about 4 times the work: 5 × 4 = 20 seconds. 10 seconds assumes the work grows in proportion to n.
steps: Worst-case comparisons = n(n − 1) ÷ 2: 1 999 000 for 2000 items and 7 998 000 for 4000 items.
That is about 4.0 times as many, so the time is about 5 × 4 = 20 seconds.

mistakes.B: Step 2: the work grows like n², so 2 times the items is about 4 times the work, not 2 times.
mistakes.C: Step 2: the comparisons grow like n², not n³ — multiply by 4, not 8.
mistakes.D: Step 1: more items means more comparisons, so the time must go up.

questions.prompt: The equation x² − 4x + 1 = 0 has a solution near 3.73. Two rearrangements are tried, both starting at x₀ = 3: xₙ₊₁ = (xₙ² + 1) ÷ 4 and xₙ₊₁ = 4 − 1 ÷ xₙ. Which one converges to the solution near 3.73?
questions.explanation: The first gives 2.5, 1.812, … drifting away (towards the other solution, about 0.27). The second gives 3.6667, 3.7273, … closing in on 3.73.
steps: Both are rearrangements of x² − 4x + 1 = 0, so test them by iterating from 3.
First rule: 2.5, then 1.812 — moving away from 3.73.
Second rule: 3.6667, then 3.7273 — moving towards 3.73, so only xₙ₊₁ = 4 − 1 ÷ xₙ works.

mistakes.A: Step 2: work out a few terms: 2.5, 1.812, … they move AWAY from 3.73.
mistakes.B: Step 2: two rearrangements of the same equation can behave very differently — test each one.
mistakes.D: Step 3: xₙ₊₁ = 4 − 1 ÷ xₙ gives 3.6667, 3.7273, … which is closing in on 3.73.
